_comment: What a FAILURE of each test costs a consumer. A passing test contributes
nothing; only failures score.
Labels are deliberately plain rather than 'fail-open'/'fail-closed'. That
vocabulary inverts across domains -- in physical security a fail-SAFE door
unlocks on power loss while a fail-SECURE one locks -- so a reader from a
safety-engineering background can read the jargon backwards. 'Reports
success anyway' cannot be misread.
The ordering is the defensible part: a control that finishes green without
doing the work is worse than one that refuses to run, because only the
first creates false assurance (Saltzer & Schroeder 1975, 'fail-safe
defaults'; CWE-636). The weights are chosen, not derived -- argue with them
here rather than in the rendering code.
Default is 'closed': a test that goes red without a declared class is
assumed to be argus breaking loudly, not argus lying.
ON THE WORD 'DEGRADED'. This file used to spend 'degraded' on 'something
alongside the scan broke, such as uploading a report'. argus PR #427
introduces ContainerScanResult.degraded for a different fact: a default
sub-scanner could not run, so the scan is THINNER than it looks. Two facts
cannot share one word on a board that reports both, so the local meaning was
renamed to 'auxiliary' and 'degraded' now tracks upstream.
They are not worth the same. An auxiliary breakage -- a SARIF upload that
failed -- leaves the scan and the gate intact, so it stays at weight 1. A
degraded scan is reduced assurance: the gate held, but over less than the
caller believes, and the difference is invisible unless the missing
sub-scanners are named. It sits at 6: above a loud refusal to run (3),
because a refusal tells you plainly that you have no result, and below a
silent pass (10), because a degraded scan at least did some of the work and
is supposed to say so.
_status_note: The word is the TEST OUTCOME, not a verdict on argus. A dashboard that
labels a product 'unsafe' on the strength of assertions its maintainers
have not agreed to is overstepping. The severity lives in the risk number,
the class counts and the sentence, all of which describe what was observed
E5 and E9 used to be called out here as known-open findings -- argus
reporting success having scanned nothing. argus PR #427 closes both with a
validate-inputs job, and that job is pure bash in container-scan.yml itself,
so it is live on a branch run rather than waiting on an SDK release. The
call-out is gone: if they go red now it is a regression, not a known state.

glossary.open: argus reported success without actually running the check. Nothing warns you, so unscanned code can ship looking approved.
glossary.degraded: argus ran, but with fewer sub-scanners than the caller asked for or expected. The gate held over less than it appears to -- and if the missing sub-scanners are not named, you cannot tell this apart from a full scan.
glossary.closed: argus stopped or errored when it should have worked. Your pipeline blocks, which is disruptive, but nothing slips past unnoticed.
glossary.auxiliary: Something alongside the scan broke, such as uploading a report. The scan itself ran at full strength and the gate held, so nothing unsafe got through.

open.line: at least one test reports success without scanning -- see the failing rows

closed.line: argus refuses to run where it should work

degraded.line: a scan ran with fewer sub-scanners than were asked for

none.line: every defined test that ran, passed

auxiliary.line: an auxiliary path is broken; scans and gates still work

index.name: Risk index
index.caveat: The weights are a judgement call, not a measurement. The number adds up rather than averaging, so adding passing tests can never lower it. Only fixing a failure does.

references.ieee: J. H. Saltzer and M. D. Schroeder, “The protection of information in computer systems,” Proc. IEEE, vol. 63, no. 9, pp. 1278–1308, Sep. 1975.
references.note: fail-safe defaults — the basis for ranking a permissive failure above a restrictive one

references.ieee: MITRE, “CWE-636: Not failing securely (‘failing open’),” Common Weakness Enumeration. [Online].
references.note: failing open is a named weakness class, not a local preference

references.ieee: National Institute of Standards and Technology, “Assessing security and privacy controls in information systems and organizations,” NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5, Jan. 2022. [Online].
references.note: control assessment is binary — satisfied or other than satisfied — which is why each test is pass/fail rather than scored

_why_open: R6, C3-C6, D3, D4, E8, S13, S14 and S18 all assert that argus FAILS a run:
a severity gate firing, a build gate firing, missing registry credentials
being rejected, an SCN category threshold being enforced. If one of them
goes red, argus let through something it was asked to stop -- the
E5 and E9 are the same class observed directly: a scan naming no
recognised scanner, and a remote scan with an empty image_ref, both report
_why_degraded: E11 and E14 are SARIF upload paths: losing them costs visibility in the
Security tab, not the scan itself. S16 is dry-run issue payloads, S25 the
optional AI fallback, U4 the SCN detector's own unit tests -- all real, none
of them a control a consumer is relying on at scan time.
